example_01.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods in the webapp namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage pod lifecycle for the web application namespace. This is a security weakness because it allows users with no need-to-know access to delete or create pods, which could lead to unintended consequences.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read access to a wide range of cluster resources, including pods, nodes, services, and namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all these resources across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_03.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments in the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can create, update, or patch deployments in the cicd namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_04.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on secrets and configmaps in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all secrets and configmaps in the database namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_05.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read access to node information and persistent volumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all nodes and persistent volumes in the cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_06.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on configmaps in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user — with no credentials at all — can write to configmaps in the logging namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on service accounts across the entire cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create service accounts in any namespace. This creates a security weakness because it allows users with minimal privileges to provision service accounts that could potentially be used for malicious purposes.

example_08.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all pods in the development namespace. Additionally, it allows creating exec sessions into pods, which could lead to unauthorized access. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_09.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on ingresses. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage ingress resources in the ingress-nginx namespace. This is a security weakness because it allows users with no need-to-know access to modify routing configurations.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to all authenticated users
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole with full administrative access within tenant namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can perform create, update, and delete operations on all resources in the namespace. This is a security weakness because it allows users who are not explicitly intended for admin tasks to have such broad permissions.

example_11.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an nginx web server workload and mounts the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods, deployments, and services in the webapp namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions for a static HTTP server workload — it can create, update, and delete resources, which is not required for serving static content.

example_12.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with excessive permissions
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Redis cache workload and its annotation states it is for application session storage. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods, deployments, and configmaps in the caching namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted excessive permissions for a workload that only needs to read and write its own configuration. This misconfiguration creates a security weakness because an attacker could exploit these permissions to manipulate other pods or deployments in the caching namespace.

example_13.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with delete permissions
example_13.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, and delete permissions on pods, deployments, services, and endpoints. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount in the monitoring namespace. However, the deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus metrics scraper workload that does not require delete permissions on these resources. Reading all three files together reveals an unnecessary risk: the service account has been granted delete access to critical cluster resources, which could be exploited by an attacker.

example_14.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static file server workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states it serves uploaded assets over HTTP, which does not require access to services, ingresses, or endpoints. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on these resources, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for such broad access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_15.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with sensitive credentials
example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database workload and mounts the postgres-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete permissions on deployments, pods, persistentvolumeclaims in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount. However, the deployment also stores sensitive credentials (POSTGRES_PASSWORD) in its environment variables. This creates a security weakness because the role grants delete permission on pods, which could be used to delete the pod and thereby expose the sensitive credentials. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together.

example_16.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a React frontend application workload and its annotation describes it as serving the user interface. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, endpoints, and deployments in the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all three files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions for a React frontend application workload — it only needs get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, endpoints, and deployments if it's intended to manage these resources itself, but this seems unlikely given its description as serving the user interface. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together.

example_17.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with excessive permissions
example_17.justification: The role.yaml grants the nginx-proxy-role Role, which has excessive permissions on pods, deployments, and services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-proxy-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted create, delete, update, and patch permissions on deployments, which is unnecessary for a reverse proxy workload. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when considering the relationships between these resources.

example_18.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary delete permissions
example_18.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, statefulsets, and pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount in the logging namespace. However, the deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch workload that only needs read access for log storage operations. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all four files together — the role file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the unnecessary delete permissions.

example_19.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_19.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and services in the messaging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. However, the deployment does not require such broad permissions for its operation — it only needs access to RabbitMQ's management interface (15672) and message queue (5672). Reading all four files together reveals that the role grants unnecessary permissions, creating a security weakness.

example_20.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_20.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete permissions on deployments in the exports namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-exporter-sa ServiceAccount. However, the deployment.yaml defines a static nginx metrics exporter workload that only exposes basic HTTP metrics endpoint and does not require such broad permissions. Reading all three files together reveals an unnecessary risk — the service account has been granted more permissions than necessary for its intended operation.

example_21.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated ingress to frontend pods
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend workload running nginx and does not explicitly require any backend API calls or credential access. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress from any pod with role: ingress-controller, which could potentially allow unauthenticated users to access the frontend pods in the webapp namespace. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for unrestricted ingress, while the network policy establishes it has been allowed exactly that.

example_22.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthorised ingress traffic from backend API
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database with sensitive credentials. The networkpolicy.yaml isolates postgres pods from unauthorised ingress traffic, but allows ingress from the backend-api pod. However, there is no clear justification for why the backend-api pod needs to access the PostgreSQL database, and this relationship creates a potential security weakness.

example_23.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus workload running prom/prometheus:v2.47.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it collects cluster telemetry. However, the role.yaml grants get access to all secrets in the monitoring namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the default ServiceAccount of the Prometheus Deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all three files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_24.category: Unnecessary service account token for a non-privileged container
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the payment-api Deployment with automountServiceAccountToken set to false. This means that the pod will not have access to the service account token, which is typically used by privileged containers or those requiring authentication. However, since this container does not require any credentials for its operation (as stated in the annotation), it should not be granted a service account token. The presence of the service account token could potentially allow unauthorized access to other resources if compromised.

example_25.category: Unnecessary service account token for Elasticsearch deployment
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch cluster and sets automountServiceAccountToken to false. However, the networkpolicy.yaml isolates Elasticsearch pods by restricting ingress to logging agents only. This suggests that the Elasticsearch deployment does not need a service account token for authentication purposes. The misconfiguration is only visible when reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for a service account token, while the network policy establishes it has been isolated from external traffic.

example_26.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthorised ingress and egress
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ message broker workload with no explicit security requirements. However, the networkpolicy.yaml creates an isolation policy for RabbitMQ pods in the messaging namespace, but it allows ingress from any pod labelled as 'app: worker' and egress to any such pod. This means that any pod with this label can potentially access or be accessed by the RabbitMQ message broker without explicit authorisation, creating a security weakness.

example_27.category: Unnecessary service account token for Jenkins deployment
example_27.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins CI/CD controller and sets automountServiceAccountToken to false. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to Jenkins pods from authorised build agents only, implying that some form of authentication or token-based access control is in place. The misconfiguration arises because the Jenkins deployment does not have a service account token mounted, which would be necessary for it to authenticate with the cluster and interact with other resources. Reading both files together reveals this discrepancy.

example_28.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for a static web server
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a React single-page application serving the user interface. However, it has automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which is unnecessary for a static web server like this one. This setting can create security risks if not properly managed.

example_29.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access from load balancers
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an API gateway workload with no explicit mention of authentication or credential access. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress and egress for the API gateway pods but allows unauthenticated access from load balancers via the ingress rule. This creates a security weakness as it enables potential attackers to enumerate internal backend services without any authentication checks.

example_30.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for worker pods
example_30.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a worker Deployment with automountServiceAccountToken set to false. This means the worker pods will not have access to any service account tokens, which is unusual because most workloads rely on these tokens for authentication and authorization. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress traffic to job scheduler pods only, but it does allow egress traffic to postgres pods. Given that the worker pods are running in the staging namespace and do not have access to any service account tokens, it is unclear what they would be trying to communicate with outside of their own pod or the job scheduler. This lack of clarity suggests that the automountServiceAccountToken setting may be unnecessary, potentially creating a security weakness if an attacker were able to exploit this configuration.

example_31.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments in the apps group. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the cicd-deploy-sa ServiceAccount in the cicd namespace. However, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole with full cluster administrative access for platform engineering team, which is bound to an unknown service account (not provided). This creates a security weakness because the cicd-deploy-sa ServiceAccount has unnecessary permissions on deployments and can potentially be used to escalate privileges to full cluster administrative access.

example_32.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with elevated permissions
example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate permissions on roles, which is a sensitive action. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the Prometheus service account in the monitoring namespace. However, the target_role.yaml defines an even more permissive Role with full administrative access within the same namespace. This creates a security weakness because the Prometheus service account now has elevated permissions due to the binding in rolebinding.yaml, and these can be further escalated by the monitoring-role-manager Role. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading all three files together.

example_33.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for API gateway service account
example_33.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate, get, and list permissions on users, serviceaccounts, and userextras. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount in the webapp namespace. This means the API gateway can impersonate any user, including those with high-privilege roles like platform-admin, which is granted cluster-admin privileges by target_clusterrolebinding.yaml. Reading all three files together reveals a security weakness: the API gateway has been granted overly broad impersonation permissions that could be used to escalate its own privileges or access sensitive information.

example_34.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a user with automated deployment permissions
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and bind permissions on roles in the rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the devops-automation-user User, which is a user with automated deployment permission management responsibilities. This creates a security weakness because the devops-role-binder Role has broad permissions that could be used for malicious purposes if the user were compromised or misused.

example_35.category: Overly broad cluster-wide read access for security audit escalator role
example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named security-audit-escalator that grants escalate permissions on clusterroles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the security-team group using a ClusterRoleBinding. However, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole named cluster-wide-reader that grants read access to all resources and non-resource URLs in the cluster. This creates a cross-resource relationship where the security audit escalator role has overly broad permissions due to its binding to the cluster-wide-reader role.

example_36.category: Overly broad impersonation of service accounts by workflow engine
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the workflow-sa-impersonator ClusterRole, which allows impersonating any service account and creating tokens for them. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the workflow-engine-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace. This means the workflow engine can impersonate any service account in the cluster, including high-privilege accounts like the cluster-provisioner-sa. Reading both files together reveals a security weakness: the workflow engine has been granted excessive privileges that could be used for malicious purposes.

example_37.category: Overly broad cluster role with administrative access
example_37.justification: The target_clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named platform-admin that grants full administrative access to all resources and non-resource URLs. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace. However, the clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole named platform-rbac-manager that allows escalation of roles for automated provisioning. This creates a security weakness because the platform-admin role has unrestricted access, which could be escalated further by the platform RBAC manager role. Reading all three files together reveals this cross-resource relationship and the potential risk.

example_38.category: Overly broad impersonation of system:masters group
example_38.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate and get/list permissions on groups and users. The target_clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the system:masters group to the cluster-admin ClusterRole, which is a highly privileged role that effectively grants full cluster access. Impersonating this group causes the API server to evaluate requests as if they were made by a cluster-admin member via normal RBAC. This impersonation is overly broad and creates a security weakness because it allows holders of system:masters to gain full cluster access, which can be recreated even after revoking the binding.

example_39.category: Overly broad cluster role granting deployment permissions to platform engineering group
example_39.justification: The role.yaml defines a ClusterRole that grants get, list, and bind permissions on cluster roles. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-engineers Group via a ClusterRoleBinding. However, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole granting broad workload deployment permissions across the cluster, including create, update, patch, and delete actions on deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets, pods, secrets, and serviceaccounts. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted to the platform engineering group.

example_40.category: Overly broad cluster role with escalate and impersonate permissions
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named tenant-admin-manager that grants escalate, impersonate, get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on various resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the tenant-provisioner-sa ServiceAccount in the tenants namespace. This creates a security weakness because the role has overly broad permissions, including escalate and impersonate, which can be used for privilege escalation attacks. Reading both files together reveals that the role is bound to a service account with no apparent need for such extensive privileges.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a nginx workload serving pre-built static HTML files only, with no backend or credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_42.category: Unnecessary secret access for metrics-only exporter
example_42.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus node exporter workload and explicitly states in its annotation that it exposes host-level hardware and OS metrics only, requiring no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the monitoring namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the node-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_43.category: Unnecessary secret access for a public-facing exporter
example_43.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the blackbox-exporter workload, which is described as probing unauthenticated public HTTP and ICMP endpoints only. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the probing namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the blackbox-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration becomes visible when reading all four files together: the deployment establishes that no secret access is required for its operation, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_44.category: Unnecessary secret access for a service with no authentication enabled
example_44.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Memcached workload and explicitly states in its annotation that it has no authentication enabled by default. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access due to its lack of authentication, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_45.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require credentials
example_45.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the StatsD exporter workload and explicitly states in its annotation that it receives StatsD metrics over UDP and exposes them as Prometheus metrics, with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the metrics namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_46.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_46.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Caddy workload serving pre-built React static assets over HTTP on port 80 only, with no TLS configuration, no backend integration, and no credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the frontend namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the caddy-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_47.category: Unnecessary secret access for Prometheus metrics exporter
example_47.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus Graphite exporter workload and explicitly states in its annotation that it receives Graphite metrics over TCP and exposes them as Prometheus metrics, with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the redis namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_48.category: Unnecessary secret access for a static health check probe
example_48.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a curl-based HTTP healthcheck probe that only polls public service endpoints and does not require any credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the staging namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the healthcheck-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration becomes visible when reading all four files together — the deployment establishes that no secret access is necessary for its workload, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_49.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_49.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Apache httpd workload serving static documentation content over HTTP only, with no dynamic backend or credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the docs namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the httpd-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_50.category: Unnecessary secret access for a diagnostic service
example_50.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the whoami workload and states it requires no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the whoami namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the whoami-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_76.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_76.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on PersistentVolumeClaims in the storage namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user — with credentials of any kind — can manage PVCs in the storage namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_77.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_77.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets across the cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all secrets in the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_78.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_78.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on NetworkPolicy resources in the API namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user — with no credentials at all — can manage NetworkPolicies in the API namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_79.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_79.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants bind access to ClusterRoles and get, list, create, update access to ClusterRoleBindings. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can bind ClusterRoles for platform administration purposes. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the clusterrole file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_80.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_80.justification: The role.yaml grants create access to ServiceAccount tokens in the staging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create ServiceAccount tokens in the staging namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_81.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_81.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Grafana dashboard workload and its annotation states it is for visualising metrics. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on configmaps and services in the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the grafana-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the Grafana workload has been granted unnecessary permissions — it only needs get, list, create, update, patch access for its operations, but the role grants delete permission as well.

example_82.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with excessive permissions
example_82.justification: The role.yaml grants the jenkins-role Role, which has excessive permissions on pods, serviceaccounts, and deployments. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the jenkins-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the Jenkins CI server workload has been granted unnecessary access to create, delete, update, and patch service accounts, as well as get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on deployments.

example_83.category: Overly broad secret access for in-memory cache service
example_83.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Memcached workload and its annotation explicitly states it is an in-memory cache. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace, as well as exec access to pods and get, list, and watch access to pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the Memcached workload has been granted overly broad secret access — it only needs read access to secrets for configuration purposes, but the role grants full CRUD permissions on all secrets in the namespace.

example_84.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_84.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a MongoDB database workload and its annotation explicitly states it requires access to persistentvolumeclaims for storage. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on persistentvolumeclaims, as well as get, list, watch, and delete permissions on deployments and pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the mongodb-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions for a MongoDB database workload — it only needs access to persistentvolumeclaims for storage, not the other resources listed in the role.

example_85.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_85.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, deployments, and pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the jaeger-sa ServiceAccount in the tracing namespace. However, the deployment.yaml defines a Jaeger workload that does not require such broad permissions — it only needs to access its own service and deployment resources for operational purposes. Reading all four files together reveals an unnecessary risk: the service account has been granted excessive permissions that could be exploited by malicious actors.

example_86.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for a container that doesn't need it
example_86.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Apache Solr search platform, but the automountServiceAccountToken is set to false. This means the solr pod will not have access to any service account tokens, which could be a security risk if other pods in the cluster rely on these tokens for authentication or authorization. However, upon closer inspection of the networkpolicy.yaml, it appears that only the search-api pod is allowed to communicate with the Solr pod, and this communication is restricted to port 8983. Given that the solr container does not need access to any service account tokens, setting automountServiceAccountToken to false seems like a reasonable security measure.

example_87.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for Kafka deployment
example_87.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Kafka message broker and sets automountServiceAccountToken to false. However, the networkpolicy.yaml isolates Kafka broker pods by restricting ingress to producers and consumers only. This suggests that the Kafka deployment does not need access to service account tokens for its operation. The misconfiguration is only visible when reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for service account token automounting, while the network policy establishes it has been isolated from other pods.

example_88.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unscoped access to Falco pods
example_88.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Falco runtime security tool monitoring system calls for threat detection. However, the networkpolicy.yaml grants ingress access to all pods with label tier: security from any pod with app: security-dashboard, which is overly broad and does not restrict access to only necessary services. This misconfiguration creates unnecessary risk by allowing unscoped access to Falco pods.

example_89.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for Envoy proxy
example_89.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Envoy proxy serving as an edge gateway for API traffic. However, the spec contains automountServiceAccountToken: false, which means the Envoy pod will not have a service account token mounted. This is unusual because most pods rely on their service account tokens to authenticate with other cluster services. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to stable version Envoy gateway pods only, but this does not change the fact that the deployment explicitly disables service account token automounting. Reading both files together reveals a potential security weakness: if the Envoy pod needs to access other cluster services for some reason (e.g., logging or metrics), it will be unable to do so without additional configuration. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_90.category: Unnecessary service account token for Jupyter notebook server
example_90.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jupyter notebook server and sets automountServiceAccountToken to false. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to Jupyter notebook pods from authorised ML platform users only, which implies that some form of authentication or token-based access control is in place. The misconfiguration arises because the Jupyter notebook server does not have a service account token mounted, despite being subject to network policy restrictions that imply some form of access control is necessary.

example_91.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to service account with platform access
example_91.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole that allows the rolebinding manager to bind existing RoleBindings and get/list namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace. However, the target_rolebinding.yaml grants full administrative access within the production namespace to the same platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount via a RoleBinding referencing the admin ClusterRole. This creates a security weakness because the platform automation service account now has broad access across multiple namespaces, including production.

example_92.category: Overly broad RBAC role with escalate permission
example_92.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate permissions on roles, which is a sensitive action. The target_role.yaml defines an overly broad data engineering role that includes the ability to create, update, and delete pods, services, secrets, configmaps, persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, statefulsets, jobs, and cronjobs. This role is bound to the data-engineers group in the rolebinding.yaml file. Reading all three files together reveals a potential security weakness: an unprivileged user in the data-engineers group could escalate their permissions to create or delete sensitive resources.

example_93.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for infrastructure automation user
example_93.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate permissions on users, serviceaccounts, and userextras. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user User. This means the infra-automation-user can impersonate any user or service account in the cluster, which is a security weakness because it allows for arbitrary access delegation.

example_94.category: Overly broad ClusterRole with full administrative access granted to a group
example_94.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole called clusterrole-binder that allows the SRE team to bind ClusterRoles for incident response access management. However, this role also grants get, list, and watch permissions on all namespaces. The target_clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole called platform-admin with full administrative access (get, list, and watch on all resources) granted to it. This is then bound to the SRE team group in the clusterrolebinding.yaml file. Reading both files together reveals that the SRE team has been granted overly broad permissions, allowing them to manage any resource in the cluster.

example_95.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with elevated privileges
example_95.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate and bind permissions on roles, as well as create, update permissions on rolebindings. This means that any pod using this service account will have elevated privileges within the ops namespace, including the ability to escalate and bind roles. However, the target_role.yaml defines a Role with full administrative access within the ops namespace, which is likely unnecessary given the already broad permissions granted by the role.yaml. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading all three files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_119.justification: The role.yaml grants read access to the database-credentials secret within the database namespace only. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the database-sa ServiceAccount within the database namespace only. Reading all two files together confirms the secret access is both necessary and appropriately scoped — the workload legitimately needs credentials for database access and access is restricted to exactly that one secret.

example_120.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a group with unknown membership
example_120.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read-only access to jobs for the ML team. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the ml-team Group within the ml namespace only. However, the misconfiguration is that the binding is to a group with unknown membership, which could potentially include users or services outside of the intended scope. This creates a security weakness because it allows access to jobs without proper control over who can actually read them.
